articles.title: Bruno Fernandes breaks silence for first time after Ronaldo’s Portugal exit, reveals direct  conversation with him
articles.summary: Bruno Fernandes speaks out about Cristiano Ronaldo's exit from the Portugal national team, asserting his status as the nation's greatest icon and emphasizing team unity.
articles.body: Cristiano Ronaldo's sudden departure from the Portugal camp has left the national team facing questions about what happens next, but one of his most prominent teammates has now made his position clear. Bruno Fernandes has spoken directly to the veteran forward and delivered an emphatic defence of Ronaldo's place in Portuguese football, while insisting that the squad remains united despite the controversy surrounding his exit.Bruno Fernandes insists Ronaldo remains Portugal's greatest iconFernandes revealed that he has remained in direct contact with Ronaldo since the forward left the Portugal camp, with the Manchester United captain making clear that he does not believe the situation should overshadow everything Ronaldo has given to the national team and the country.“I spoke with Cristiano and told him that he is and will always remain the GREATEST icon of our national team and our country. Our national team is united, not divided. Matters must be resolved internally and conclude well for both parties,” Fernandes said.The comments come as uncertainty continues to surround Ronaldo's future with Portugal after the 41-year-old made the decision to leave the squad during the Nations League campaign.Ronaldo's departure followed Portugal's 2–1 victory over Norway, during which the five-time Ballon d'Or winner remained an unused substitute after warming up during the match.The decision marked the first time in 18 years that Ronaldo had been left out of a competitive starting lineup and then not brought onto the pitch, adding to the tension surrounding his role under head coach Jorge Jesus.Ronaldo's relationship with Jorge Jesus at centre of disputeThe circumstances surrounding Ronaldo's departure have increasingly centred on his relationship with Jesus, with the forward reportedly holding discussions with the 72-year-old coach and senior figures within the Portuguese Football Federation after the Norway match.Those discussions ultimately failed to prevent Ronaldo from leaving the national team camp, with the Al-Nassr forward later confirming his decision in a statement posted publicly.“After the press conference of the national team and following a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp. In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave.”Ronaldo has not yet provided that fuller explanation, leaving the circumstances of his departure open to further discussion while Portugal continue their Nations League campaign without their long-time captain.Ronaldo's exit sparks social media falloutThe fallout has extended beyond the Portugal training camp, with reports claiming that the Portuguese Football Federation's official Instagram account lost more than one million followers during the 24 hours after Ronaldo's departure became public.Ronaldo himself then appeared to add another layer to the situation by liking a social media post that criticised the way the federation and coaching staff had handled his recent involvement with the national team.The Portuguese Football Federation responded to the growing reaction with a brief statement focused on the team's immediate responsibilities rather than the controversy surrounding Ronaldo's departure.“The entire delegation remains fully focused on the national team’s upcoming commitments and achieving the defined objectives,” the federation said.Fernandes' intervention has now provided one of the clearest public messages from inside the Portugal camp, with the Manchester United captain making his view of Ronaldo's standing unmistakable while calling for the dispute to be resolved internally.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Canelo Álvarez, 'traicionado' por México: su nefasta apuesta ante Estados Unidos
articles.standfirst: El boxeador mexicano tenía una confianza ciega en la Selección Mexicana en el partido que cayeron por 3-0 ante USMNT
articles.summary: El boxeador mexicano tenía una confianza ciega en la Selección Mexicana en el partido que cayeron por 3-0 ante USMNT
articles.body: Saúl "Canelo" Álvarez se va de vacío en su apuesta deportiva en la que quería mostrar su verdadera afición por la Selección Mexicana, algo que no es la primera vez que hace el boxeador con el combinado nacional. Su última 'aventura' apostando del boxeador fue en el Clásico de la Concacaf, en el tercer partido del inicio de la era de Rafael Márquez. A través de sus redes sociales, el Canelo había presumido su confianza con el Tri y mostró una fuerte apuesta realizada a favor de los dirigidos por Rafa Márquez. Canelo apostó la exorbitante cantidad de 7.182,72 dólares (ya que la plataforma es extranjera), que equivale a 130.449 pesos mexicanos. Mientras llega el día de su pelea ante el francés Christian Mbilli, el sábado 31 de octubre de 2026 en Riad, Arabia Saudita, Saúl Álvarez se arriesgó, y perdió apostándole ‘unos pesos’ al triunfo del equipo nacional. Estados Unidos le ganó a México por un contundente 3-0 en una nueva edición del Clásico de la Concacaf, en el State Farm Stadium de Glendale, Arizona, en un partido de preparación que representa el 80.º enfrentamiento histórico entre ambas selecciones. México llegó a este encuentro tras empatar 1-1 ante Perú, resultado que dejó al equipo de Márquez con dos empates en sus primeros dos encuentros de esta nueva etapa. Estados Unidos, por su parte, vive también una etapa de reconstrucción bajo las órdenes de Mauricio Pochettino. El conjunto estadounidense llega con una mezcla de futbolistas experimentados y jóvenes, después de una convocatoria de 28 jugadores para esta Fecha FIFA. El técnico argentino todavía busca consolidar su proyecto rumbo a los próximos compromisos oficiales.

articles.title: College football winners and losers: The Big Ten's depth looks even shallower in 2026. Will that be a College Football Playoff problem?
articles.summary: There are legitimate national title contenders in the Big Ten. But then there's a big dropoff.
articles.body:
The Big Ten's bragging rights over the SEC are well-earned. When you win the last three national championships, you have the right to chirp a little bit.

Though it's getting harder and harder to see if the Big Ten will be able to keep chirping for a fourth consecutive offseason.

Sure, Ohio State is one of the best teams in the country. The No. 5 Buckeyes showed it in an easy 31-14 win over No. 14 Iowa. No. 6 Indiana doesn't look as indefatigable as it did a season ago, but the Hoosiers are still really, really good.

But after Ohio State and Indiana … who else are you comfortable considering a national title contender?

The obvious answer is No. 15 Oregon, but the Ducks already have a loss to their name and, unfortunately, a question at quarterback after Dante Moore's concussion. Head injuries are serious and can be finicky. Whatever is best for Moore's health should be the priority, even if it means an extended absence.

Even with Moore at 100% sooner rather than later, Oregon is operating without much margin for error. A loss at Ohio State on Nov. 7 is about all Oregon can afford to still comfortably make the playoff.

Behind those three teams, there's No. 18 USC, who escaped a late comeback attempt from Washington on Saturday night. But we're at the point where you need to see a big win from USC to believe in the Trojans as anything more than a second-tier team in the Big Ten.

And after USC, there's No. 23 UCLA, a feel-good story in the making under new head coach Bob Chesney. He led James Madison to the College Football Playoff a year ago. And just two ranked teams remain on UCLA's schedule the rest of the season.

That preceding sentence, however, is a damning statement about the quality of the rest of the conference.

The Big Ten has been a top-heavy league in recent seasons and it's at the risk of tipping over this year. Michigan and Penn State are both 0-2 in conference play after losses to Minnesota and Northwestern, respectively, in Week 5. Illinois, a team that won 19 games over the past two seasons, is also 0-2 and lost to Purdue on Saturday. Purdue! The Boilermakers last won a Big Ten game in 2023.

Teams like Minnesota, Nebraska or even Wisconsin could turn into surprise contenders this season. We're not going to rule that out. But if we were making a combined top 15 between teams from the Big Ten and SEC, we're not sure we'd have more than five Big Ten teams in that group.

Will that be a problem in the postseason? The Big Ten's relative lack of depth hasn't proven to be one in the last three years. But it also may be shallower than ever in 2026. We went on record with Oregon as our title pick before the season and aren't ready to abandon that choice just yet. But it's also impossible not to see how the SEC's title odds are increasing simply because the conference has more teams who could earn the opportunity to make a deep playoff run.

Here are the rest of this week's winners and losers.

Purdue: The Boilermakers finally have a win over a power conference team. Purdue went to Illinois and won 24-17. It was Purdue's first win over an FBS team in over a year and, well, just look at how long it had been since Purdue had beaten a Big Ten team.

Boilermaker football has been in the abyss for a long time. Purdue is still one of the worst programs in the Big Ten, but there are at least signs of life now. Illinois, meanwhile, what the heck is going on?

Northwestern: The first game at the brand-new Ryan Field couldn't have gone much better. The Wildcats had Penn State's run defense in a blender in a 34-13 win over the Nittany Lions to christen the team's new stadium. Caleb Komolafe rushed for 188 yards on 25 carries while Joseph Himon II had 162 yards and two scores on just 10 rushes. Northwestern rushed 55 times for 413 yards in total. Penn State, meanwhile, had just 291 total yards a week after losing at home to Wisconsin.

Florida State: This was a score that looked like one from the late 1990s or early 2000s for the Seminoles. Never mind that this iteration of FSU closed as a slight home underdog. Florida State beat Virginia 38-7 as QB Ashton Daniels rushed 17 times for 136 yards and five touchdowns.

The defense was also a terror, as Florida State sacked Virginia QB Beau Pribula 10 times. It was a nightmarish game for a Virginia offense that had scored at least 27 points in each of its first four games of the season.

Pitt: The Panthers will be ranked in the AP Top 25 on Sunday after a 35-33 victory over Virginia Tech. However, that win did come at a significant cost. QB Mason Heintschel suffered a torn right ACL when he was hit while sliding, and he'll miss the rest of the season.

Holden Geriner takes over as the Panthers' starter and there's a decent chance that Pitt can get to 7-0 before playing Miami later this month. The Panthers' next two games are against North Carolina and Boston College. And games against Georgia Tech, Florida State, Louisville and Cal after that don't look as daunting as they could have. Pitt would be a formidable ACC contender with a healthy Heintschel. The potential for a very good season is still there though.

NDSU: Are the Bison really going to win the Mountain West in their first season at the top level of college football? The Bison are now 5-0 overall and 2-0 in the MWC after a 28-0 home win over Wyoming. The Bison are allowing less than 10 points per game and QB Nathan Hayes added a rushing element Saturday that he hadn't yet provided. Hayes rushed 10 times for 79 yards and two scores.

Michigan: What is there to say about the Wolverines' offensive output so far this season? Name a pessimistic adjective and it applies. Michigan hasn't scored more than 19 points in any of its four games against opponents who aren't UTEP and had just two first-half touchdowns in a 20-14 loss to Minnesota on Saturday. Three second-half turnovers doomed the Wolverines, though those could have been overcome if the Michigan offense could have sniffed the end zone. The 180 yards Michigan had against Minnesota is by far a season low.

West Virginia: Mountaineers coach Rich Rodriguez was one exasperated man about his defense after WVU's 45-42 loss at Iowa State.

Iowa State had 29 first downs and 577 yards of offense in the win as running back Aiden Flora rushed 22 times for 212 yards and scored five total touchdowns. The lackluster defense overshadowed West Virginia's own offensive effort; West Virginia had 518 total yards on just 63 plays. But the Mountaineers also fumbled twice in the second half, including on their final drive.

Louisville: Are things unraveling early for the Cardinals? After losing on a last-second field goal to Ole Miss in Week 1 and then beating SMU by 10 in Week 3, Louisville has lost two straight games. On Saturday, the Cardinals fell 31-28 to NC State as Wolfpack QB CJ Bailey threw for 373 yards and two scores. Louisville QB Lincoln Kienholz is banged up — he took the field with heavily taped ankles and was not the rushing threat that he typically is. But Louisville fumbled three times to detract from the 213 yards on 17 combined carries from running backs Isaac Brown and Keyjuan Brown.

Western Kentucky: A program that has won at least eight games in each of the last five seasons now sits at 1-4 after a 34-13 loss at New Mexico State on Friday night. The Hilltoppers' only win so far this season came over Mercyhurst and they haven't scored more than 20 points against an FBS opponent across the other four games. Yes, two of the losses came at Georgia and at Indiana, but games at Nevada and New Mexico State are ones that WKU typically wins. Instead, they were losses by a combined 56 points.

South Carolina: The Gamecocks have played two SEC home games. They have built early two-touchdown leads in both of them. They have lost both of them. The latest loss came Saturday in a 35-34 overtime defeat to No. 24 Kentucky. South Carolina led 17-0 early, before failing to close out the Gamecocks in the second half and then giving up the game-winning 2-point conversion in overtime. South Carolina is now 0-3 in the SEC a year after going 1-7 in conference play.

articles.title: Colorado State Fires DC Tyson Summers, Jim Mora Explains Mid-Game Controversy After Loss vs. OSU
articles.summary: Colorado State head coach Jim Mora announced Saturday that defensive coordinator Tyson Summers is no longer with the team following the 56-26 loss against Oregon State.
articles.body:
Colorado State head coach Jim Mora announced Saturday that defensive coordinator Tyson Summers is no longer with the team following the 56-26 loss against Oregon State.

Mora said that Summers "left the field" after he was demoted during the game and Kenny McClendon took over the defensive play-calling. ESPN's Pete Thamel reported that Summers wasn't fired during the game, though Mora confirmed that Summers is no longer with the program:

After starting 2-0, the Rams have lost three straight, giving up an average of 52 points per game in defeats against BYU, UTSA and Oregon State.

Beavers' quarterback Braden Atkinson shredded the Colorado State defense on Saturday to the tune of 413 yards and five touchdowns through the air, completing 30 of 34 passes. That came one week after UTSA put up 542 yards of total offense and 59 points on the Rams' defense, and two weeks after BYU rushed for a staggering 332 yards against them.

Summers, 46, was in his second stint as the school's defensive coordinator, a role he first held for a season in 2015 before becoming the head coach at Georgia Southern. He returned to Fort Collins in 2025 as the defensive coordinator and also operated as the interim head coach for five games after Jay Norvell was fired.

Mora was then hired and kept Summers aboard to lead the defense. It was a short relationship, however, and there was plenty of foreshadowing that a divorce was inevitable—leading into this week's matchup against Oregon State, Mora made it abundantly clear that he was expecting Summers to simplify his defensive scheme.

"Players at any level, regardless of intelligence, can only comprehend so much in a football game. It's chaos," he told reporters . "When you get in situations where your players aren't playing fast because they're not certain, it's critically important that you shrink the package."

"That's why I say we have to do a better job. We can't wait to change things. It's too late and that's not fair to our players," he added. "You have to be ultra-demanding of your players but you have to be specific about what you're demanding of them. It's not easy. It's complicated, but we have to un-complicate it."

That apparently didn't happen to Mora's liking, to the point that Summers is no longer with the program.

articles.title: Misery Index: Is Penn State already regretting ditching James Franklin for Matt Campbell?
articles.summary: Penn State AD Pat Kraft may already be feeling the heat after the Nittany Lions lost a second straight Big Ten game to a team it was supposed to beat.
articles.body:
If you could turn the clock back to Oct. 12, 2025, the day Penn State fired James Franklin, and tell Nittany Lions fans everything that would happen over the next 51 weeks, it would be interesting to know how many of them would want a do-over.

Because as frustrating as Franklin could be, and as shocking as it was to be 3-3 last October with a team that was considered a national title contender, nobody really imagined this — least of all athletic director Pat Kraft.

If you knew Penn State's coaching search would go on for more than 50 days, with a whole bunch of rejections before landing on Matt Campbell, would it have been the right decision?

If you knew that the highly rated recruiting class Franklin assembled would go up in smoke and be replaced by a bunch of transfers Campbell brought with him from Iowa State, would it have been worth making a change?

And if you knew that Campbell's first five games would include losses to Wisconsin and Northwestern — teams that went a combined 11-14 last season — how tempting would it be to sneak into Kraft's office, steal his cell phone and laptop and make sure that he had no method of communication to the outside world for the rest of the season?

This isn't to suggest that it was a definite mistake to fire Franklin. Kraft's reasons for wanting a change were valid, and it's too early to say that Campbell can't get the job done.

But in the moment? Yeah, it looks bad. Really, really bad. So bad that Kraft is going to feel the full wrath of Penn State's fan base after Friday night's 34-13 loss to Northwestern and deserves every bit of scrutiny that will come his way the rest of this season.

Because when you defy convention to fire a coach just six games after he led your program to College Football Playoff semifinals in 2024, and when you think you can do better than someone who went 104-45 and consistently had Penn State in the top 15, you better be right.

Even if you're a fan who lacked faith that Franklin was going to deliver a national title, and even if you're an administrator who grew weary of his excuses for not winning enough big ones, he did not have to be fired. Though last season blew up in Franklin's face with a team that seriously underperformed during the bizarre three-week stretch that sealed his fate, Kraft made a proactive choice to change coaches before it was obviously necessary.

It was a gamble, a bet that Penn State was a big enough brand with attractive enough resources to make a coaching upgrade.

And though the search eventually landed on a logical choice with a great reputation — even NFL teams had poked around about Campbell's availability during his time at Iowa State — Penn State is a different kind of job than anywhere he'd coached before.

Tougher conference, greater scrutiny, more demanding fan base, much higher stakes.

And while we must stress that it's still early to make definitive statements about how Campbell will work out in the end, getting pushed around by Northwestern is a massive red flag. Penn State got outgained 506-291. Even if this is a good version of Northwestern, that should never happen.

"I put a lot on me because there's somehow, some way I didn't get this team prepared to play the physical brand of football we need to play," Campbell said after the game.

Well, it's too late now for this season. A lot of prognosticators picked Penn State to be a playoff contender because of a friendly Big Ten schedule, and in some ways it's even easier now than it looked in the preseason with teams like Michigan and Washington among the biggest early-season disappointments.

But no matter what Penn State does the rest of this year, the what-ifs and recriminations will hound Kraft unless Campbell can prove next season that he's the right guy for the job.

That's a lot of pressure, but it's also what Kraft signed up for when he got rid of a successful coach under the premise that he could hire a better one. And it's why Penn State reigns as America's most miserable fan base in Week 5.

ACC: It is an undeniably cool story that Andrew Luck returned to Stanford, where he was one of the great players in school history, to lead the program as general manager. It's really the only reason anyone has paid attention to Stanford football over the last couple seasons, and it's generated plenty of fawning media coverage. But there is no on-field evidence yet that Luck knows what he's doing in this role. Nobody is going to argue that life is easy for Stanford, which is stuck in an ACC that doesn't fit geographically and can't fix its roster quickly with transfers because of the school's academic requirements. Still, losing 57-3 to Wake Forest — one of the ACC's other academic powers — is a result that might truly represent rock bottom for a program that was contending for national titles just over a decade ago. Nobody expects that anymore from Stanford, but this is a program that hasn't won more than four games in a season since 2018. And Luck's selection of 39-year-old Tavita Pritchard as head coach has gotten off to a rocky start. Pritchard, the former Stanford quarterback, was on staff for some great years under David Shaw before going to the NFL as an assistant coach. But since Luck took over, Stanford has lost by three touchdowns or more eight times in 17 games. That's not sustainable.

Big 12: Watching West Virginia's 45-42 loss to Iowa State was reminiscent of those Big 12 games from a decade ago when it felt like nobody in the conference had even a slight interest in playing defense. Until the final possession, when West Virginia's DJ Epps fumbled along the sideline after crossing into Iowa State territory, the teams combined to score on six straight possessions. That included a 63-yard touchdown run and a 75-yard touchdown drive for Iowa State in the fourth quarter with no resistance at all from the Mountaineers. After allowing a ridiculous 577 yards, coach Rich Rodriguez told reporters his team had "some key problems to a level that I haven't seen in awhile," adding it's "stuff that I haven't seen in years" and calling it "hard to watch." Other than that, things seem fine in West Virginia, which will face high-powered offenses in Arizona and Cincinnati in the next two weeks. After a 3-0 start to the season, including an upset over Virginia, it looked like the Mountaineers might be a sneaky CFP contender. Instead, the 63-year-old Rodriguez is 2-9 in Big 12 games during this second stint in Morgantown.

SEC: With a little more than six minutes left, and trailing Tennessee by three points, Auburn coach Alex Golesh decided to go for a fourth-and-1 from his own 24-yard line. Even though there was plenty of time left and he was risking the game right then and there, going for it was a defensible choice. The ensuing play call, however, was not. The Vols were not fooled at all by Auburn's choice to pitch the ball backward to Omar Mabson and tackled him behind the line of scrimmage, giving them a short field to land the knockout-blow touchdown in a 24-14 victory. It was also emblematic of the concerns Auburn fans have about the Golesh regime during this 3-2 start. Golesh, who made his reputation as an offensive coordinator under Josh Heupel at Tennessee and then as head coach at South Florida, is not scoring enough points or playing the kind of physical football that wins in the SEC through his first five games. The personnel and play-calling are just not up to par for what Auburn needs to win in this league. Golesh chose to bring a bunch of players with him from USF, including quarterback Byrum Brown, but that's a stop-gap measure at best. Auburn needs a lot more SEC-quality talent to compete at this level.

Group of Six: Few programs outside the power conferences generate as much "sleeping giant" buzz as Colorado State. With its prime location, a great stadium, a history of success under Sonny Lubick in the 1990s and enough resources to win big in the new Pac-12, Colorado State's potential was enough to lure Jim Mora Jr. away from UConn this year. But so far, it looks like the same old story after an embarrassing 56-26 loss at home to Oregon State. The Rams have given up a boatload of points this season, including 59 in a loss to UTSA, 41 to BYU and even 24 to Southern Utah. That will put a spotlight on Mora's decision to retain defensive coordinator Tyson Summers, who took over as interim head coach last season after Jay Norvell was fired and went 0-5. ESPN reported shortly after the game ended that Summers had been dismissed and was stripped of his play-calling duties during the game . For all its potential, Colorado State looks like it might be headed for its eighth losing season in the past nine years. The school invests too much in football to keep taking this many losses.

Shane Beamer: For a coach who knew this season was going to determine his future, losing 35-34 in overtime to Kentucky is a gut punch that might be impossible to recover from. South Carolina led this game 17-0 early in the second quarter, held a 27-24 lead through most of the fourth quarter until Kentucky tied it with about four minutes left and scored first in overtime to take a 34-27 lead. It still wasn't enough, as the Wildcats won on a gutsy 2-point conversion call by first-year Kentucky coach Will Stein. At 2-3, it's hard to figure out how South Carolina turns this around with a trip to Florida next Saturday before a bye week. Beamer was so close to getting South Carolina into the CFP in 2024, but winning just one out of 10 SEC games since then isn't good enough. Gamecock fans love Beamer's feistiness and don't demand perfection, but we all know what happens when the bottom falls out like this.

Kyle Whittingham: Since the NIL era began, there may be no greater example of big money being lit on fire than Michigan's recruitment of Bryce Underwood. Funded by a group including Jolin Zhu (wife of Larry Ellison) and Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy, the deal that got Underwood to de-commit from LSU and pick Michigan instead was worth a reported $3 million a year for four years. That wasn't Whittingham's decision, but it's now his problem because Underwood just has not progressed in two years at Michigan and it's killing any chance of putting a functional offense on the field. After a 20-14 loss at Minnesota, a game in which Underwood completed just 10-of-21 passes for 101 yards and two interceptions, Whittingham called the current state of Michigan football "the biggest challenge I've had" in more than 40 years of coaching. Though the Wolverines are only seven total points from being unbeaten rather than 3-2, remember that they were a Hail Mary touchdown (and a clock controversy) away from losing to Western Michigan, as well, and haven't reached 20 points against anyone except UTEP. It's certainly fair to question whether the 66-year-old Whittingham was the right guy for Michigan at such a late stage in his career after two decades at a lower-profile job in Utah. But inheriting a quarterback who isn't going to live up to the massive contract he got out of high school has put Whittingham in a pretty rough position out of the gate — and he may need to pull the plug on Underwood if there's any hope of saving this season.

Jeff Brohm: The knock on Brohm is that the moment you start to buy in, his teams will lose one that boggles the mind. It happened last season when Louisville was up to No. 15 and got beat at home by Cal, which ended up firing its coach. It happened in 2024 against a bad Stanford team after the Cardinals climbed into the top 25. And it's happened this year in back-to-back weeks with losses to Wake Forest and NC State that will knock Louisville completely out of the playoff picture. You might scoff at invoking the P-word, but the combination of a favorable schedule and Louisville looking good early, with a close loss to Ole Miss and a win over SMU, made it seem possible. Instead, Louisville is now 2-3 after a 31-28 loss to NC State in which its offense committed three turnovers and its defense allowed 493 yards. The Brohm cycle of high highs and unimaginably low lows continues.

Virginia Tech's optical disillusion: Even on Saturday morning, after they'd watched dozens of replays from all kinds of angles, it wasn't hard to find Hokies fans on social media who were absolutely convinced that John Love's 36-yard field goal attempt as time expired should have been called good instead of wide left, leaving Virginia Tech on the wrong side Friday night of a 35-33 loss to Pitt. To be fair, there are some angles where it looks like the ball might have snuck inside the upright. But there are other angles you can find where the arc of the kick pretty clearly shows it hooked wide as it crossed over the top of the left upright. The lesson here is two-fold. First, short of some type of technology that would tell us definitively, nobody is going to have a better view than the referee standing under the goal, and he was emphatic that the kick missed. The second lesson is also simple: A 36-yard field goal is short enough, and Love is a good enough kicker, that it should never have been that close in the first place. And for Virginia Tech, it's hard to blame the kick or a referee's call when you commit four turnovers at home and lose a game in which you had a 499-295 advantage in yards.

UCF's loss of space: Going back to their days in the American Conference, the UCF-Houston rivalry is about space as much as football. Outer space, that is. With its proximity to Cape Canaveral and the school's original mission to educate future employees of the Kennedy Space Center, UCF has claimed the title of Space U. But Houston, of course, is known as "Space City" because it also has a strong NASA connection. As former Houston coach Dana Holgorsen said a few years back, "They don't say, 'Orlando, we've got a problem.'" So who won the space race this time? The Cougars, wearing special "Gridiron Galaxy" helmets and blue uniforms, came back from a 17-0 deficit and scored 27 straight points in the final 19 minutes of the game to win. UCF is now 3-8 in Big 12 games since Scott Frost returned and hasn't been able to claim college football's space crown since 2023.

UConn's rough(ing) rivalry: After erasing a 34-14 deficit against Syracuse, UConn needed to stop only one more play in overtime from the 17-yard line to celebrate its first win over the Orange since 2011. Though the rivalry between schools was based mostly on their Big East basketball battles, it's still a matchup with huge emotional stakes for both sides because the fan bases don't like each other very much. And when UConn not only gave up a 17-yard touchdown pass on fourth down but committed a roughing-the-passer penalty as well, it was about as bad a sequence of events as UConn has ever had in the football rivalry. With the ball moved to the 1 1/2 yard line, Syracuse coach Fran Brown had no choice but to go for two and the victory. When quarterback Amari Odom stretched the ball over the goal line, it somehow felt like UConn had given away a game it probably never should have been in position to win in the first place.

articles.body: Argentina goleó por 7-0 a Burkina Faso en un amistoso surrealista marcado por los problemas de la selección africana. Burkina Faso llegó a Buenos Aires sólo seis horas antes del comienzo del partido tras un vuelo de 11 horas desde Casablanca. Ante la negativa de la selección absoluta a viajar a Argentina por problemas con la organización del vuelo y ciertas cuestiones financieras, Burkina Faso se ha visto obligada a jugar con el equipo Sub-23 en un amistoso bochornoso de principio a fin. Con goles de Lautaro Martínez (m.3), Moumouni Diallo, en propia meta (m.8). Gianluca Prestianni (m.12), Nicolás Paz (m.35), Julián Álvarez (m.36), Franco Mastantuono (m.57) y Giuliano Simeone (m. 91), Argentina pudo meter tantos goles como hubiese querido a una Burkina Faso que tuvo una posesión del 25% y sólo realizó un disparo a puerta en todo el partido. Especialmente dramáticos fueron los primeros 15 minutos de partido con un penalti a favor de Argentina en el minuto 4 (lo falló Lautaro Martínez aunque luego marcó en el rechace del portero), un gol en propia meta de Burkina Faso en el minuto 8 y un tanto de Prestianni en el minuto 12. Argentina se fue ganando 5-0 al descanso tras dos goles en un minuto: Nico Paz en el minuto 35 y Julián Alvarez en el 36. "Agradecerle a Burkina Faso, a los que han venido por el esfuerzo que han hecho. Dignifican al futbol, nosotros intentamos jugar el partido como si fuera una final porque así es la única manera de que estos chicos fueran respetados. Agradecemos el esfuerzo de que hayan podido venir, se podrían haber quedado y el partido se hubiera suspendido. Es muy rescatable lo que han hecho. Un vuelo tan largo y llegar a la hora que llegaron y jugar... No es fácil". En el segundo tiempo, Scaloni rotó todo el banquillo (portero incluido) e hizo debutar a tres jugadores nuevos con Argentina: Matías Soulé, Tomás Palacios y Santiago Castro. Tras este bochorno, Argentina se prepara ya para la despedida de Leo Messi en su último partido con la albiceleste. Será la noche del martes ante Benín en el Estadio Monumental de Buenos Aires. "El partido del martes me lo imagino muy emotivo, para todo el mundo, incluido Leo, será un día inolvidable. Será su día, y el de sus compañeros, que también le dieron su mayor alegría futbolística. Agradezco poder disfrutarlo", reconoció Scaloni en rueda de prensa. articles.title: Yahoo Top 10: SEC parity is peaking, and it's made for a messy few weeks
articles.summary: There weren't too many upsets in Week 5, but there were plenty of standout performances.
articles.body:
On Saturday, Alabama beat Mississippi State, which beat Missouri, which beat Florida, which beat Ole Miss, which beat LSU, which … you get the point.

The parity in all of college football, especially within the SEC, seems to be at its peak — a product of the transfer and athlete compensation changes within the sport. Competitive NIL and free transfer movement has loosened the stranglehold that the historical big brands have on the sport.

But it does make a midseason ranking a difficult task. Florida slips from our poll yet Ole Miss remains (barely). Missouri is unranked and Mississippi State drops out of the poll, too. It paves the way for newbies like Tennessee (hey now, the Vols kept pace with top-ranked Texas last week) and Indiana (we know — they haven't played anybody!).

Things will eventually sort themselves out.

Speaking of sorting, did you catch Friday night's results? Pitt stormed back to beat Virginia Tech to move to 5-0 and coach Pat Narduzzi was demanding the team be ranked . Also, Northwestern opened its stadium with a banger of a beatdown over Penn State (perhaps Matt Campbell's rebuild will take some time ).

Minnesota beat Michigan at home for the first time since the 1970s (it was PJ Fleck's first win over the Wolverines in 10 years with the Gophers), Ohio State drilled Iowa in a Kinnick Stadium beatdown and Purdue got its first Big Ten win in over 1,000 days at Illinois.

As far as the hot seat goes, Mike Norvell helped his case (FSU whipped Virginia) while Shane Beamer (Kentucky beat South Carolina in OT) and Mike Locksley (Maryland blew a lead at Nebraska) hurt theirs.

The Longhorns have two of the best wins in the country (Ohio State and at Tennessee). QB Arch Manning and crew got a much-needed rest this week before the annual battle with the Sooners in Dallas. Plenty of teams have a solid argument for the No. 1 spot, but Steve Sarkisian and Co. keep top honors for another week. Can Texas hold on? Its next five opponents after Oklahoma are all ranked in the current AP Top 25, including top-10 teams Florida and Ole Miss in back-to-back weeks.

At this point, it's getting quite ridiculous with Jeremiah Smith. Has any receiver in college football history had such a start to the season like this one: 617 yards over five games with seven touchdowns and 33 catches. His 11-catch, 206-yard Saturday at Kinnick Stadium broke open a fairly tight first three quarters. The Hawkeyes didn't have near the firepower to keep pace with Ohio State, and their defense finally faltered late. You can't corral Smith for long!

The Hurricanes look big, fast and physical. Could they be better than last year's version that advanced to the national championship game? While QB Darian Mensah and WR Malachi Toney get the attention, Miami's offensive and defensive lines, as well as battering ram back Mark Fletcher, are the real MVPs. And don't forget about another weapon, Cooper Barkate, the former Harvard receiver who transferred to Duke and then Miami with Mensah this offseason.

Bulldogs QB Kamario Taylor stole the pregame spotlight for much of this week. Alabama QB Keelon Russell stole the in-game spotlight. Russell threw for 285 yards and three touchdowns as the Crimson Tide crushed Mississippi State with an impressive, full-team beatdown (the defense had a pick 6). The most impressive stat was Russell's third-down numbers: 6-for-7 passing for 146 yards and two scores. Time to start talking about Russell and the Tide's championship chances.

One of the early storylines this season has been Notre Dame's struggles to run the ball. Well, Jonaz Walton raced for 120 yards on 23 carries in Chapel Hill and QB CJ Carr threw four touchdowns. The Tar Heels moved the ball at times against the Irish — a bit concerning — but this one never felt too much in doubt given Carr's efficiency (21 for 29). If in doubt, he can bail you out with his big arm (39- and 28-yard touchdowns).

Are we sleeping on QB Gunner Stockton? He's not been prolific this season so far (probably because he doesn't have to be), but he's tossed 10 touchdowns and one interception. And he was prolific on Saturday against Vanderbilt, with 295 yards passing while completing 78.1 percent of his passes. Kirby Smart's defense is good again (what else is new!?). The Commodores had a single drive of more than 35 yards. Up next? A trip to Tuscaloosa.

The Vols have some serious problems to attend to, including a quarterback situation that turned south on Saturday. Josh Heupel benched true freshman Faizon Brandon for backup George MacIntyre, who completed 8 of 10 passes in an ugly game where Tennessee trailed 7-3 at the half. The Vols' defense did enough, and so too did RB DeSean Bishop, whose 230 yards, 34 carries and three touchdowns made the difference in this one. Remember, Tennessee hung around with top-ranked Texas, which beat Ohio State. The Vols D is legit.

You may be surprised to see the Utes here in the Top 10 but they beat the brakes off of Arkansas (I know, the Hogs aren't very good) and then whipped Iowa State in Ames. It's not the toughest schedule in the country, no. But QB Devon Dampier and first-year coach Morgan Scalley have done enough to, for now, earn their way into the rankings, especially compared to many other challengers that "haven't played nobody," as they often say.

The Hoosiers' best opponent so far is Northwestern, but they break into our rankings after an impressive pulverizing of the Scarlet Knights. TCU QB Josh Hoover tossed four touchdowns. He's got 15 on the season now and hasn't thrown an interception. We're about to find out real soon how legit Indiana is. IU travels next week to Nebraska for their first opponent with a real pulse.

Last time we saw the Rebels they didn't look much like a top-10 team as they were getting run over and around by the Florida Gators. But don't write off Pete Golding's team yet. Don't forget that they've still got one of the nation's best quarterbacks (perhaps the best QB) in Trinidad Chambliss. But did the Rebs use the off week to shore up that defense? We sure hope so. Two ranked opponents, Missouri and Texas, are next up.

articles.title: Estevao, Pedro and Samuel Lino expose India’s shortcomings as Brazil cruise to 4-0 victory in Kolkata
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Brazil 4 and India 0.
articles.body: KOLKATA: Brazil 4 and India 0. The staggering gap between the five-time world champions and the one with 137 Fifa ranking and hardly any international pedigree of late looked too obvious to mention.If goalkeeper Gurpreet Singh Sandhu was partially responsible for allowing Brazil to go 2-0 up in the first half, with Estevao and Pedro finding the target in 28 and 42 minutes, Samuel Lino’s brace as a second-half substitute, in 58 and 90+5 minutes, were quite pleasing to the eye. The result was unapologetically direct. This was also a reminder that when the game as a contest melted into a foregone conclusiona, the line between reverie and reality got blurred and the gap in class and quality between the two sides looked as large as the geographical distance between the countries.In Brazil’s rebuilding process, this match perhaps lacked the usual significance and substance and was more about paying homage to their massive fan base in this part of the world. In India’s transitional phase, this didn’t even come with its conventional contour of something to fight for but rather as an eerily abstract way of negotiating a challenge they didn’t have the wherewithal to survive, let alone rescuing anything from it.Yet, despite odds heavily stacked against them, India got in on the act initially with conviction, trying hard to prevent it from falling victim to formula. There were some moments, however transitory they might have been, when a sense of expectations drifted in the air. Apuia’s snap shot from the distance, Manvir Singh runs and a couple of Ryan Williams’ attempts elicited roars of appreciation from the crowd. Those were the times when energy got blended with purpose in Indian players’ footsteps and embraced the possibility of matching the South American giants with a fearlessly combative mentality. On occasions when Vinicius and Pedro and others came calling with their usual attacking aspirations, they were stopped in their tracks by some well-executed offside traps from Anwar Ali and Co.However, two poor judgments allowed Brazil to make the script look familiar. When Estevao, facing a challenge from Ashique Kuruniyan, let fly a powerful left-footer, the India goalkeeper wearing the captain’s armband, couldn’t hold on to it.Soon Pedro, who replaced injured Barcelona star Raphinha in Carlos Ancelotti’s line-up, saw his header hit the post. And when the Flamengo star, who was ignored for Brazil’s World Cup squad, latched on to Estevao’s brilliant through-ball, Gurpreet was again found wanting in closing out the space and couldn’t prevent the ball from rolling into the net.It could’ve been more before the break but Vinicius couldn’t beat Gurpreet from a one-on-one situation.Khalid Jamil was forced to replace Gurpreet with Prabhsukhan Gill at the second half. Ancelotti also came out with a slew of substitutions, including one to introduce Samuel in place of Vinicius. The Flamengo attacker, a key member of Ancelotti’s rebuilding Brazil, found the target twice with the kind of precision that was enough to wow the crowd.In the end, India did exhibit some moments of resolve. articles.title: Juicio a Jorge Jesus
articles.standfirst: Portugal se enfrenta a Noruega en el primer partido en casa desde el 'caso Cristiano Ronaldo'
articles.summary: Portugal se enfrenta a Noruega en el primer partido en casa desde el 'caso Cristiano Ronaldo'
articles.body: El primer partido de Jorge Jesus en casa desde 'el caso Cristiano Ronaldo' será esta noche (20.45h, ante Noruega)... y en territorio hostil para el veterano técnico. Él, que fue entrenador del Benfica y el Sporting CP, ocupará el banquillo local de Do Dragao, en Oporto. De su boca, sin embargo, solamente salen mensajes de unidad: “El cariño que busco y deseo no es otro que el que siento por la selección nacional. Ese cariño es para el equipo, no para mí. Soy parte de un equipo, soy el líder”. Una filosofía que comparte Bruno Fernandes, uno de los líderes del vestuario: “Lo más importante es que esto termine bien para ambas partes. Lo que pido es que el país no se divida, que no tome decisiones, que respete a todas las partes, pero, al mismo tiempo, Cris es y será el mayor ícono de nuestra Selección Nacional, se merece el respeto de todos, independientemente de a quién le guste más o menos”. Ambos intentaron no dar demasiada importancia a lo ocurrido fuera del terreno de juego con el que, hasta hace unos días, era su capitán. “Cristiano Ronaldo es un símbolo de la selección nacional, de Portugal. Después del partido, habrá tiempo de sobra para hablar de ello”, analizó el seleccionador. “Respecto a Cristiano, hablé con él, y lo que le dije, y lo que repito aquí, es esto: lo más importante es que, pase lo que pase, Cristiano Ronaldo nunca dejará de ser el mayor símbolo de nuestra selección nacional, de nuestro fútbol y del país, por lo que ha hecho no solo en Portugal sino en todo el mundo”, fueron las palabras de Bruno. El partido, más allá de lo futbolístico y su trascendencia en la clasificación, pues si gana Portugal estará matemáticamente en el play-off de la Nations League, servirá como referéndum público para que la afición lusa se exprese sobre lo ocurrido con Cristiano. Para Noruega, mientras, este partido representa una necesidad. Los de Solbakken, una de las sorpresas en el Mundial 2026 tras alcanzar los cuartos de final eliminando a Brasil, están contra las cuerdas. Los nórdicos suman tres puntos después de haber encajado dos derrotas en los dos últimos partidos de este parón: Gales... y Portugal, en Oslo, en el duelo que hizo estallar 'el caso CR7'. El triunfo sobre Dinamarca (3-2), ya lejano, es lo único que les da un poco de aire para seguir pensando en no pelear por no bajar de categoría en esta Nations. Solbakken, mientras, hará cambios y el más notorio se espera en la portería: Egil Selvik apunta a ocupar el puesto de Nyland, discutido tras haber encajado Noruega seis goles en tres partidos de este parón.

articles.title: 'Soft goals, individual errors, many mistakes': Khalid Jamil rues India’s 4-0 loss to Brazil
articles.summary: KOLATA: All the pre-match talk was about the huge gulf between the two teams; one that has played every edition of the FIFA World Cup, won five, and even
articles.body: KOLATA: All the pre-match talk was about the huge gulf between the two teams; one that has played every edition of the FIFA World Cup, won five, and even though they are now far from their best, still ranked sixth in the world.India’s rankings in football have been an embarrassment. At last count, it was 137.Everyone wondered at the mismatch. In Brazil, particularly, the ridicule was evident. “If you don't win 20x0 ag-ainst that nonexistent Indian squad, you might as well not even come back to Brazil -- just stay there,” one fan posted on X. When the match kicked off, another one remarked, “20 minutes and you can’t even score against India.”Without moving out of second gear, Brazil eventually won the friendly 4-0 at the Salt Lake Stadium here on Saturday, but coach Carlo Ancelotti admitted it wasn’t easy at the start. “We had difficulty in opening the score, but the moment Estevao scored, we had more opportunities,” said Ancelotti. “We felt good (playing in India). It was a good experience. India played their part, tried to defend, played counterattack. It was a positive game.”Three of India’s four goals could have been avoided. There were defensive lapses, too, both individual and as a team, prompting coach Khalid Jamil to replace goalkeeper and captain Gurpreet Singh Sandhu at half time.“I think two or three were soft goals, individual errors,” said Jamil. “Many mistakes. We made a lot of substitutions, tried everyone, but they were not up to the mark. articles.title: 'Caso Negreira': la condena social y la verdad jurídica
articles.summary: Sin ataduras
articles.body: Sé que hay cosas mucho más importantes en los tribunales y en el Juzgado de Instrucción 1 de Barcelona, pero por salud y limpieza mental sería bueno que el ‘caso Negreira’ acabara cuanto antes. Sea la que sea la sentencia, esta mancha social ya no se la quitará el Barça nunca. La verdad jurídica será una y la evidencia otra. La verdad jurídica puede ser que no demuestre la clave del asunto, pero la evidencia social es innegable. Cuatro presidentes durante 17 años, pagaron más de siete millones de euros, al sistema Negreira que era vicepresidente de los árbitros. Y cuando éste, dejó de cobrar remitió un burofax al club con una torpeza temeraria para dejar rastro por escrito, además de las transferencias emitidas y recibidas, que encima Negreira no declaraba, para hacer el asunto más chusquero todavía. Bartomeu fue el que lo cortó y Laporta el que dobló los pagos. Gaspart y Rosell completan los cuatro presidentes que autorizaron bajo sus mandatos pagar a Negreira. ¿Se imaginan que se demuestra que el PSOE o el PP o un Gobierno presidido por cualquiera de ellos, pagan desde hace 18 años a Marchena del Supremo o Conde Pumpido del Constitucional o a sus hijos por informes jurídicos? La gravedad está en pensar que eso se puede hacer y autorizarlo. O saberlo y no cortarlo. Es evidente que los presidentes del Barça fueron conscientes de todo y lo autorizaron, o bien por si acaso cortarlo podría perjudicarles o bien porque como dijo Laporta en la COPE, medio justificando el asunto “el Real Madrid no hacía falta que pagara nada porque ellos ya tenían la ternera”. La intención era: por si acaso esto sirve para tener influencia a nuestro favor, vamos a pagar o a seguir pagando. Esta mancha afea el “mes que un club” del Barça y deja indefensos a cientos de miles de barcelonistas que son objeto de burla o ridículo por sus amigos, colegas o rivales madridistas. No seré yo el que trate de conexionar los éxitos de aquella época dorada del mejor Messi y la colección de excelentes jugadores, con que ganaban partidos y títulos por Enríquez Negreira. Eso es ridículo. Como ridículo es pensar que los árbitros favorecen siempre al Real Madrid. Quedarse en esas simplezas es de bajo nivel. Lo que sí está claro es que la influencia y el miedo que ejercen mediáticamente Barça y Madrid, estoy seguro que en algo condicionan a su favor a los árbitros, mucho más que al Alavés, al Valladolid o al Levante. El Barça no puede reconocer la evidencia, porque necesita mantener una posición jurídica. De hecho los cuatro expresidentes se reunieron para acordar una línea de declaraciones unificada: “Pagábamos por informes arbitrales “. Lo feo es que esos informes no se los encargaran a exárbitros, sino al vicepresidente en activo del Comité de Arbitros y a su hijo. Haciendo un símil hipotético: lo feo es que el Gobierno pagara por informes jurídicos al vicepresidente del Tribunal Constitucional y a su hijo, cuando ese organismo es quién está dando una amnistía a Puigdemont de quien depende que el Gobierno tenga mayoría para poder seguir en sus puestos. Estas cosas quebrarían la confianza en el sistema y no se pueden hacer, ni autorizar ni aceptar. El Barça que no es una persona, sino que su imagen depende de lo que decidan sus dirigentes temporales, jamás se quitará ya esta mancha social, con independencia de la verdad jurídica y de la sentencia que se emita. Luis Enrique y Valverde han declarado que ellos no sabían que existían, ni utilizaban dichos informes. Ni ellos ni nadie de su cuerpo técnico. No tiene sentido por tanto estar pagando por algo que luego no utilizan quienes deben y para quienes se hacen esos informes: para el entrenador del Barça. Sin embargo, Carlos Naval, histórico delegado del Barça, declaró en sede judicial, que sí los recibía y que los ponía en conocimiento del cuerpo técnico. Enorme contradicción con los entrenadores. De ahí que ya veremos cual es la verdad jurídica del asunto. Incluso Gerard Lopez, siendo técnico del filial afirmó en una entrevista en Onda Cero que también los recibía y que le eran super útiles. Ahora irá a declarar al juzgado. Por tanto aquí tenemos tres ámbitos: - El social: la condena es firme y evidente. - El jurídico: está por ver - La UEFA La UEFA tiene sus propias normas y se lo está tomando con calma desde 2023 que se conoció este tema. La UEFA puede decidir (digan lo que digan los tribunales españoles) su propia sentencia en base a sus artículos 4.02 y 4.04. Otra cosa es que quieran esperar a ver que sentencia hay, pero si quisieran podrían no esperar y sus inspectores ya llevan tres años y medio con conocimiento del tema. El miedo lógico que tiene el Barça es que le excluyan temporalmente de la Champions. No le va a favorecer a los blaugranas el actual caso City, aunque sea interno de la Premier Legue. El Barça además suma al ‘caso Negreira’, el de las palancas bluf que hace que el club esté con patrimonio neto negativo y ya haya sido sancionado por la UEFA con 15 millones de multa y con aviso de mayor sanción si no corregía sus números. Justo acaba de hacer otra pirueta contable para ello. Políticamente el Barça ha estado (en su época de noviazgo con Florentino y la Superliga) enfrente de la UEFA muchos años. Ahora se ha bajado del barco y Florentino en una evidente conveniencia se convierte ahora ante la UEFA en un puñal acusatorio contra el Barça por el ‘caso Negreira’. Pero lo hace ahora, porque se siente vacilado y traicionado por Laporta al salirse de la Superliga. La UEFA le tendrá ganas a Florentino seguro. Y a la misma vez no tener en contra al Real Madrid como club, le supone un descanso. Esta semana se ha desempolvado el asunto porque la propia UEFA ha comunicado que ha recibido el famoso dosier de Florentino por Negreira. Ese comunicado no necesario, me suena a un gesto de hacerle una caricia al Real Madrid para darle importancia, sabedor del tortazo que le ha supuesto a Florentino rendirse sin condiciones de la Superliga. La jueza de Barcelona tampoco ha admitido que se alargue 6 meses más la instrucción del caso como pedía Florentino. Que a nadie se le olvide que Tebas fue mucho más contundente y rápido que Florentino para irse al juzgado contra el Barça en este asunto. A los seis días de conocerse el ‘caso Negreira’, LaLiga denunció los hechos a la Fiscalía de Barcelona (20 febrero 2023).. El 10 de marzo la Fiscalía de Barcelona presentó denuncia ante el juzgado. Y sólo dos días después (y un mes y medio mas tarde que LaLiga) el Real Madrid se personó en la causa, pero ya lo hizo por vergüenza ajena de quedarse con los brazos cruzados. Todavía era época de amor entre los dos. Florentino sólo se ha activado con potencia ahora, a raíz de traicionarle Laporta en la Superliga, hasta el punto que en pleno romance el presidente del Madrid llegó a contestar a un socio que pedía romper relaciones con el Barça que “… con el Barça hay que llevarse bien, son amigos y nos necesitamos, aunque seamos rivales en el campo “. Me genera más curiosidad el desenlace final en la UEFA, que el del juzgado. Por los mismos motivos que lo hace ahora la Premier, la UEFA ya sancionó en febrero de 2020 al City, a 30 millones de multa y dos temporadas excluido de jugar Champions. Sin embargo, el TAS (como el TAD en España) anuló en Julio de ese mismo año, las dos sanciones, alegando que “no existía prueba concluyente suficiente y que parte de las infracciones estaban prescritas”.

articles.title: Cavan Sullivan becomes youngest USMNT goal scorer in win over Mexico
articles.summary: Julian Hall scored for the third straight game and Malik Tillman added a late goal as the Americans won their third straight.
articles.body:
GLENDALE, Ariz. — Soccer friendlies are, by definition, inconsequential affairs. U.S.-Mexico entanglements, however, are special under any circumstances.

And at the start of a new World Cup cycle, with some 3 ½ years to expand and mold his roster, Mauricio Pochettino used Saturday's 3-0 romp at rocking State Farm Stadium to discover how his young Americans would fare in the boiler of this savage regional rivalry.

In front of a near-capacity crowd disproportionately sporting Mexican green, two attackers with a combined age of 35 scored in each half as Pochettino's second term continued on its stirring path with a third consecutive victory.

Julian Hall, 18, became the first U.S. player since Eddie Johnson 22 years ago to score in his first three appearances and Cavan Sullivan, who turned 17 on Monday, became the youngest scorer in U.S. history — breaking a record set by Mathis Albert, 17, on Tuesday.

For the rest of the match, Mexican fans mocked their failing goalkeeper.

Diego Kochen, 20, went the distance in goal for the Americans and made a terrific reflex save when the U.S. led by one.

Malik Tillman, a two-goal scorer at the World Cup, added the third goal against a defensively ragged Mexican side seeking its first victory since the World Cup.

The Americans will close the extended international window Tuesday against Canada in St. Paul.

Pochettino's lineup selections were largely expected, with one surprise: Kochen, the former Barcelona prospect who debuted in the second half of the Peru match last weekend.

He got the nod over Matt Freese, the World Cup starter who was in the lineup for the window opener against Peru. He hadn't done anything glaringly wrong in that 4-1 victory, but with Kochen's stock rising in U.S. circles ahead of the 2028 Olympics, Pochettino wanted to test him in an intense match.

Chris Richards and Auston Trusty manned central defense, while Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman were the wing backs. Captain Tyler Adams and Sebastian Berhalter supported Gio Reyna and Tillman in midfield.

Sullivan had freedom on the right flank, looking to combine with Hall, who had won the striker job after posting two goals and an assist (plus a wonderful dummy on a goal-scoring sequence) in 99 minutes over two matches.

Under new coach Rafa Márquez, Mexico opened the window with 1-1 draws against Colombia and Peru. El Tri will wrap up camp against Chile on Tuesday in Los Angeles.

Gilberto Mora, the 17-year-old star reportedly drawing interest from Barcelona, Real Madrid and Liverpool, was not in uniform after hurting his ankle on Tuesday, spoiling hope of a teenage showdown between Mora and Sullivan.

Márquez started eight players with at least 30 caps. Every starter, except teenager Santiago Sandoval, was between 24 and 32 years old. With his 128th cap, defender Jesús Gallardo had logged more appearances than seven U.S. starters combined.

El Tri set the early terms. Kochen didn't need to make any saves but did have to play the ball with his feet while under pressure from Mexico's forwards.

Tillman provided an early thrill for the U.S., making an individual run into the penalty area that resulted in a pair of harmless corner kicks. Sullivan was pesky and deceptive on the right side, but for the most part, the U.S. labored to sustain possession in the attacking half.

That all changed in the 28th minute when the Americans connected 17 passes.

Mexico was willing to allow them to interact harmlessly in midfield. Berhalter then took the initiative, delivering a long ball to Freeman near the sideline. A channel opened for Reyna to make a run from a deep position. Freeman supplied him.

Rushing inside the penalty area, Reyna crossed. Goalkeeper Raúl Rangel stabbed it with his right foot but left the ball for Hall to deposit from inside the 6-yard box.

Mexico came close to drawing level late in the half when Kochen pushed a cross to Santiago Giménez's feet, but the striker sent it wide of the open net.

Moments into the second half, Reyna and Tillman unlocked the Mexican defense with a sublime combination. Tillman backheeled into Reyna's path for a cross beyond a teammate's reach.

Kochen was tested for the first time in the 58th minute, leaping to touch Roberto Alvarado's thumping drive over the crossbar.

Hall and Sullivan were about to be removed from the match when Sullivan scored — thanks in large part to Rangel, whose dreadful pass was intercepted by the Philadelphia Union star. Sullivan instinctively looked to shoot right away, chipping the ball from some 35 yards into the vacant net.

He and Hall then left, as planned, to a loud ovation.

Mexican frustration boiled over in the 67th minute. Substitute Mateo Chavez took down Yunus Musah with a hard tackle. Berhalter confronted Chavez, who responded by clapping Berhalter on both cheeks. A melee ensued — a common sight in a U.S.-Mexico match.

Tillman added the third goal in the 84th minute, beating lackadaisical defender Diego Campillo to the back pass in the box and beating Rangel to the near side for his seventh international goal.

The Americans have scored 11 goals in these three victories — an impressive tally for a mix of veterans and prospects finding their way together.

Defender Miles Robinson and goalkeeper Chris Brady were not in uniform, keeping with Pochettino's plans to dress 26 players. …

The proposed U.S.-Jamaica friendly on Dec. 13 is tentatively slated to be played in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, per sources. The match would conclude a week-long U.S. camp primarily for MLS players in a non-FIFA window.

articles.summary: El centrocampista brasileño criticó el trato humano del técnico neerlandés durante su etapa en el United, además de su relación con Cristiano
articles.body: El brasileño Fred, que coincidió con Erik ten Hag en el Manchester United antes de marcharse al Fenerbahçe, no tuvo reparos en dar abierta su opinión sobre el neerlandés en su etapa al frente de los 'red devils'. Aunque el centrocampista no dudó en reconocer la preparación táctica del entrenador, su crítica hacia la gestión de las relaciones personales dentro del equipo fue tajante: "Ten Hag tácticamente era muy bueno, pero con el grupo era un pedazo de mierda". Según Fred, las fricciones del técnico con los miembros del plantel eran constantes y terminaron por enrarecer el ambiente en la plantilla. "Discutía con todo el mundo. Discutió conmigo, con Cristiano, con Casemiro, con Rashford. No me ponía a jugar y a veces la situación resultaba estresante", detalló el futbolista a 'Charla Podcast'. No sólo eso. El internacional con Brasil también acusó al técnico de favorecer a ciertos futbolistas por su origen: "Sólo jugaban sus jugadores neerlandeses. Era un entrenador de grupitos. Pero, tácticamente, uno de los mejores con los que he trabajado". Durante la entrevista, Fred también desveló el detonante de la fractura definitiva entre Ten Hag y Cristiano Ronaldo: "Quería que el equipo corriera, pero Cristiano ya era mayor. Lo sacó del once titular y ahí hubo un desencuentro. Antes de un partido, Ten Hag dijo que Ronaldo se iba a marchar. De acuerdo, no podíamos hacer nada. Después del partido, cuando aterrizó el avión, el personal de comunicación del club quitó el modo avión y vio que había dado aquella entrevista en la que criticaba mucho al club".

articles.title: The Newcastle United heroes and villains of the 2020s
articles.summary: Here at The Mag we invited a number of regular/irregular contributors to give us their Newcastle United heroes and villains. Our thanks to David Hutchinson (...
articles.body:
Here at The Mag we invited a number of regular/irregular contributors to give us their Newcastle United heroes and villains.

Our thanks to David Hutchinson (you can hear Hutch every week on The Mag Podcast , along with Simon and Jamie, discussing all things NUFC) for taking up the challenge.

Hutch has focused on the Newcastle United heroes and villains of the current decade, the 2020s.

In truth, there are a lot of people you could put here. The obvious one is Eddie Howe. Then there are the likes of Bruno G, Trippier and even Amanda Staveley to consider. However, after consideration I went with someone who I believe is well on his way to legendary status at the club.

Dan Burn, local lad from Blyth, came into Newcastle United at the very end of January 2022 from Brighton and, at the time, I recall being a bit disappointed. A move for Sven Botman had been heavily rumoured and the big worry was that we needed more to improve upon what had been a very lacklustre defence. What an idiot I was.

His four and a half years at Newcastle have been quite something.

In the absence of an injured Trippier he stabilised a defence that looked certain for the drop. He was an ever present in helping us back into the Champions League. Once there, he scored against PSG in their SJP demolition, pocketing Mbappe in the process. Jumping ahead, have you ever seen someone score a curling header in the Champions League? I have – Dan Burn! Then there is the small matter of scoring our first goal in a domestic cup final since 1976. Helping us win our first domestic cup since 1955 and finally, becoming club captain at the age of thirty-four.

I cannot imagine in the later part of this decade anyone will have the impact that Big Dan Burn has had.

Under Steve Bruce, I recall people around me bemoaning the contributions of Jacob Murphy. Even now, he does not get the respect he deserves. With important goals and assists to his name – as well as some of the funniest banter ever seen on a football pitch – Jacob Murphy is very deserving of being my cult hero.

I suspect that this series will see many contributors opt for Steve Bruce and Mike Ashley as nominations here, but their impact on the club during this particular decade was fleeting. I have opted instead for the pantomime villain… Alexander Isak . After all, we are going to spend the next few seasons booing him relentlessly (if he is ever fit enough to play against Newcastle United again).

Not so obvious Newcastle United Villain of the 2020s

I am going to preface this by saying that an honourable mention goes to Paul Mitchell. His decision to walk out on the club led to what was one of the worst transfer windows in memory and easily the worst of the decade.

My not so obvious villain are the social media transfer influencers. This lot have crafted a niche by driving the market, hyping fans, and pressurising club boards into negotiations.

The Germans have a saying about Football. 'Die wichtigste Nebensache der Welt' – translated: it is the most important minor thing in the world. As such, we care more than we should and an attack on the club you support very much feels like an attack on you and yours.

Going back to the key 2025 summer transfer window, these transfer social influencers spent the entire summer cutting and pasting transfer stories about Isak and all the strikers we were looking at to replace him. This in turn riled the braying masses who used every post to debase the club and attack its supporters. Attack us. It felt relentless. It felt damaging, both to the club and on a personal level. And this all came on the back of our most successful season in a generation.

Of course, if has happened every transfer window since and will continue to play its part unless regulations are introduced to stop it. It is one of the worst aspects of modern football and should be consigned to the nothing.

Ep 8: Manchester City's charges, Newcastle United Women win and Drinking in the stands

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for their quality unfiltered Newcastle United debate.
